text.p: Computer Learning Centers Inc said Monday it will challenge the U.S. Department of Education's denial of the company's Chicago Learning Center's appeal of 1991 and 1993 student loan default rates.
As a result of the denial, Computer Learning said, its Chicago center has been terminated from the Title IV Federal Family Education Loan (FFEL) and the Federal Pell Grant (Pell) programs.
The company said it received notification late on Friday from the Education Department that its Chicago center was unsuccessful in its appeal.

The Education Department also notified the company it may apply to restore eligibility in the FFEL program on October 1, 1997. As is customarily the case with default rate appeals, the department provided no additional data concerning the reasons the appeal was unsuccessful, Computer Learning noted.

The loss of eligibility affects only the Chicago Learning Center, which accounted for about 11 percent of the company's revenues for fiscal 1996. The company noted its Chicago Learning Center remains eligible to participate in the Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant program and the Federal Perkins loan program.

"While we are disappointed in the loss of FFEL loan and Pell Grant funding eligibility, we intend to keep the Chicago Learning Center open at our downtown Chicago location and we feel positive about our ability to operate the Chicago Learning Center in a self-funding mode until we can reapply on October 1, 1997, for reinstatement into the FFEL program," chief executive Reid Bechtle said.
"We will continue to provide our Chicago students with financing options comparable to what they would have received under traditional federal loan programs."

He said "This will be accomplished by combinations of CLC funding and funding from private sources, as well as by shifting to the Chicago Learning Center in accordance with applicable law, SEOG and Perkins Loan funds presently allocated among our ten other Learning Centers."

Bechtle added that the law requiring an institution to cease participating in the Federal Pell Grant program if it exceeds the cohort default rate limits for participation in the FFEL programs expires on June 30, 1997, and that he expected the company to seek resumption of Pell Grant program participation immediately thereafter.

Computer Learning also said it is initiating legal action against the Education Department to compel recognition of the company's 1994 cohort default rate of 20.1 percent as representing the most recent cohort default rate data.

The department issued the 1994 rate to the Chicago Learning Center in June 1996, but maintains that the rate is not final until published by the Secretary of Education later this year. Use of the 1994 cohort default rate would mean that the school's three most recent cohort default rates were not all over 25 percent, thereby restoring the Chicago Learning Center's eligibility to the programs, the company explained.

Computer Learning said it is also challenging the department's denial of the Chicago Center's appeal, which it claimed was based on errors in the servicing of student loans by lenders and guaranty agencies. Under federal law, improperly serviced student loans may not be charged against an institution's calculated cohort default rate.
